questions.question: Explain how the alpha particle scattering results led Rutherford to conclude that the atom has a central charge in a very small volume.
questions.answer: Most alpha particles pass straight through, but a few are deflected through large angles, which needs a small, dense, positive central charge.
steps: Most alpha particles pass through the foil with little deflection, so most of the atom is empty space.
A few alpha particles are deflected through large angles, and some are reflected back.
Large deflections need a strong repulsive force from concentrated positive charge.
So the positive charge must be concentrated in a very small volume at the centre of the atom.

questions.question: Discuss why the alpha scattering observations could not show whether the central charge of the atom is positive or negative.
questions.answer: The size of the deflection depends on the magnitude of the force (charge squared), not its sign, so attraction or repulsion gives the same angle distribution.
steps: The alpha particle is positive, so a positive nucleus repels it and a negative nucleus attracts it.
Attraction bends the alpha particle towards the nucleus, repulsion bends it away, through the same magnitude of angle.
The scattering depends on the product of the charges, so the magnitude of the force is the same for +Ze and -Ze.
Only the direction of deflection would differ, and the observations (counts at each angle) could not show this sign.

questions.question: An alpha particle with kinetic energy 6.29 MeV approaches a platinum nucleus (proton number 78) head on and is repelled. Calculate the minimum distance between them, treating both as point charges.
steps: At closest approach all kinetic energy is stored as electric potential energy: E k = k Q q / r.
Charges: alpha Q = 2e = 3.2 x 10^-19 C, platinum nucleus q = 78e = 1.25 x 10^-17 C.

questions.question: Which expression gives the base units of the farad? A: C V^-1; B: C^2 J^-1; C: kg^-1 m^-2 A^2 s^4; D: kg^-1 m^-2 s^-2 C^-2.
steps: Farad = C / V, and the volt is J / C, so farad = C^2 / J.
Charge C = A s, so C^2 = A^2 s^2.
Joule = kg m^2 s^-2, so farad = A^2 s^2 / (kg m^2 s^-2) = kg^-1 m^-2 A^2 s^4.
This matches option C.

questions.question: A student writes the decay of a neutron as n -> p + e^- + neutrino (no bar shown in text). Which conservation law is violated? A: baryon number; B: charge; C: energy; D: lepton number.
questions.answer: D: lepton number
steps: Baryon number: 1 on each side, so it is conserved.
Charge: 0 = (+1) + (-1) + 0, so it is conserved.
Lepton number: the electron gives +1, and the neutrino written without a bar also gives +1, so the total is +2 instead of 0.
The correct product is an electron antineutrino, so the student has broken lepton number conservation.

questions.question: A gamma photon of energy 18 MeV produces a particle and its antiparticle. Which gives the maximum possible mass of the particle in kg? (Options are not in the text.)

questions.question: Which equation correctly shows neutron decay? A: n -> p + e^+ + (missing); B: n -> p + e^+ + nu_e; C: n -> p + e^- + (missing); D: n -> p + e^- + nu_e. (Bars on antiparticle symbols are lost in the text.)
questions.answer: D: n -> p + e^- + antineutrino (the correct beta-minus decay)
steps: Charge: 0 on the left, so the right must give +1 - 1 = 0, which needs an electron (-1).
Baryon number: 1 on each side, so neutron decay gives a proton.
Lepton number: the electron has +1, so an antineutrino (-1) is needed to balance it.
Option D has electron plus antineutrino, which is the correct decay.

questions.question: Name the process in which a low energy positron collides with an electron to produce a pair of gamma photons.
questions.answer: Annihilation (electron-positron annihilation)
steps: The positron and electron are particle and antiparticle.
When they meet, their mass is converted into energy in the form of two gamma photons: this is annihilation.

questions.question: A low energy positron and electron annihilate to produce a pair of gamma photons travelling in opposite directions. Calculate the maximum wavelength of the photons.
questions.answer: Maximum wavelength = 2.4 x 10^-12 m
steps: For low kinetic energy, the photon energy is the rest energy of each particle: E = m c^2.
Maximum wavelength corresponds to minimum photon energy, so the kinetic energies are taken as zero.

questions.question: Zweig proposed fundamental particles called aces with baryon number 1/3 and fractional charge; baryons are three aces and mesons are two aces, with four aces to match four leptons. Compare this model with the standard model.
questions.answer: Zweig's aces are like quarks (fractional charge, baryon number 1/3), but the standard model has six quarks in three generations matching six leptons, not four aces.
steps: Similarity: aces have fractional charge and baryon number 1/3, like quarks.
Similarity: baryons are three-particle combinations and mesons are particle-antiparticle pairs in the standard model (Zweig's mesons are two aces).
Difference: the standard model has six quarks (up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom), not four aces.
Difference: the standard model matches six leptons in three generations, so the quark number was not four.

questions.question: A positron has kinetic energy 23 MeV, assumed to be all of its energy. Show that it must be travelling at a relativistic speed.
questions.answer: Its kinetic energy is about 45 times its rest energy (gamma about 46), so v is about 0.99999c, which is relativistic.
steps: Rest energy of a positron: m c^2 = 9.11 x 10^-31 x (3.00 x 10^8)^2 = 0.511 MeV.
Kinetic energy is 23 MeV, which is about 45 times the rest energy.
v = c sqrt(1 - 1/gamma^2) = 0.99999 c, so the speed is relativistic.

questions.question: A positron and an electron, each travelling at 1.5 x 10^7 m s^-1 in opposite directions, annihilate to produce gamma radiation. Calculate the frequency of the gamma radiation.
questions.answer: Frequency = 1.2 x 10^20 Hz per photon
steps: Total energy = 2 m c^2 + 2 x (1/2 m v^2) since both particles are non-relativistic.
Kinetic energy each: 0.5 x 9.11 x 10^-31 x (1.5 x 10^7)^2 = 1.0 x 10^-16 J, so the total is 2.05 x 10^-16 J (negligible against 1.64 x 10^-13 J of rest energy).
Total energy = 1.64 x 10^-13 J, shared between two gamma photons, so each has E = 8.21 x 10^-14 J.

questions.question: A stationary anti-neutron decays by emitting a positron. Explain how energy is conserved in this decay.
questions.answer: The rest energy of the anti-neutron equals the total rest energy plus kinetic energy of the products.
steps: The stationary anti-neutron has rest energy m c^2 and no kinetic energy.
After decay the rest energies of the products plus their kinetic energies must add up to the original rest energy.
The mass difference is therefore released as kinetic energy of the positron and other products.

questions.question: Muons travelling at 0.994c fell 1600 m, and 74% of those detected at 1600 m reached the bottom. The muon rest lifetime is 2.2 x 10^-6 s. Explain whether the observations are consistent with relativity, with a calculation.
questions.answer: Yes: time dilation gives gamma = 9.1 and a survival fraction of about 77%, close to the observed 74%. Without relativity the fraction would be only about 9%.
steps: Without relativity: t / tau = 5.37 / 2.2 = 2.44, so the fraction surviving is exp(-2.44) = 0.087, about 9%.
With relativity: gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - 0.994^2) = 9.1, so the lifetime is 9.1 x 2.2 x 10^-6 = 2.0 x 10^-5 s.
Surviving fraction = exp(-5.37 x 10^-6 / 2.0 x 10^-5) = exp(-0.27) = 0.77, about 77%.
This is close to the observed 74%, so the observations are consistent with time dilation.

questions.question: After muons were discovered they were called mu mesons. Explain why muons are not described as mesons in the standard model.
questions.answer: A meson is made of a quark and an antiquark, but the muon is a lepton with no quark structure and is a fundamental particle.
steps: Mesons are composite particles made of a quark and an antiquark.
The muon is a fundamental lepton, with no quark structure.
So it is classified as a lepton (second generation), not a meson.

questions.question: Explain the role of electric and magnetic fields in producing high speed charged particles in a cyclotron.
questions.answer: The alternating electric field in the gap between the dees accelerates particles each half turn, and the magnetic field makes them move in circles so they return to the gap.
steps: The magnetic field acts at right angles to the velocity, giving a centripetal force that makes particles move in circles inside the dees.
The alternating p.d. across the gap produces an electric field that accelerates particles each time they cross the gap.
The p.d. frequency matches the cyclotron frequency f = B q / (2 pi m), which does not depend on speed.
Each acceleration increases speed and radius, so particles spiral outward.
Inside the dees there is no electric field, so speed only changes in the gap.
The particles leave at maximum radius with high kinetic energy.

questions.question: A positive pion with momentum 1.2 x 10^-19 N s decays into a muon with momentum 0.75 x 10^-19 N s at 18 degrees to the pion direction and a neutrino with momentum 0.54 x 10^-19 N s. Deduce whether the data are consistent with conservation of momentum.
questions.answer: Consistent: the neutrino momentum needed to balance the pion and muon is 0.54 x 10^-19 N s, matching the given value.
steps: Take the pion direction as the x-axis, with momentum 1.2 x 10^-19 N s.
Muon components: x = 0.75 cos 18 = 0.713, y = 0.75 sin 18 = 0.232 (units 10^-19 N s).
Neutrino must equal pion minus muon: x = 1.2 - 0.713 = 0.487, y = -0.232.
Magnitude = sqrt(0.487^2 + 0.232^2) = 0.54 x 10^-19 N s, equal to the given neutrino momentum.
A scaled vector diagram closes in the same way, so momentum is conserved.

questions.question: Explain why a linac with drift tubes of increasing length works with a constant frequency a.c. supply.
questions.answer: Each tube length is chosen so the particle takes half a period to cross it; as it speeds up, longer tubes keep this timing with a fixed frequency.
steps: The field is only present in the gaps between tubes, and it reverses each half cycle.
The particle must cross each tube in exactly one half period, so the field reverses correctly at each gap.
As the particle speeds up, each tube must be longer (length = speed x half period).
A constant frequency therefore works with the increasing lengths.

questions.question: A positron and an electron each of energy 14.5 GeV collide and produce two omega baryons. Calculate the kinetic energy of one omega baryon.
steps: Total energy in the collision = 2 x 14.5 = 29 GeV, shared equally by the two omega baryons, so each has 14.5 GeV total energy.
Rest energy of one omega baryon = 1.7 GeV (from part (i)).
Kinetic energy = 14.5 - 1.7 = 12.8 GeV.

questions.question: A student suggests that the collision cannot produce two omega baryons because a conservation law is broken. Discuss the student's suggestion.
questions.answer: The student is correct: two omega baryons give baryon number +2 and charge -2 (each is -1), but the initial state has baryon number 0 and charge 0.
steps: Initial state: an electron and a positron, so total charge 0 and baryon number 0.
Each omega baryon has baryon number +1 and charge -1 (standard values).
Two omega baryons would give baryon number +2 and charge -2, which breaks baryon number and charge conservation.
So the student's suggestion is correct.

questions.question: The ionised atom travels 0.2 m perpendicular to the plates before colliding with another atom. Deduce whether the collision could cause further ionisation, given ionisation energy 3.9 x 10^-19 J.

questions.question: State three observations and the corresponding conclusions from the alpha particle scattering experiment with thin gold foil.

Observation: a small number are deflected through large angles. Conclusion: the positive charge is concentrated in a small nucleus.
Observation: very few are reflected back. Conclusion: the nucleus is very dense and contains most of the atom's mass.

questions.topic: Omega Baryon Charge And Baryon Number
questions.question: A negative K meson collides with a stationary proton and produces an omega baryon and a positive K meson. Deduce the charge and baryon number of the omega particle.
questions.answer: Charge = -1 (i.e. -e); baryon number = +1
steps: Charge: initial = (-1) + (+1) = 0; final = Q_omega + (+1), so Q_omega = -1.
Baryon number: initial = 0 (K meson) + 1 (proton) = 1; final = B_omega, so B_omega = +1.
The omega particle therefore has charge -1 and baryon number +1.

questions.question: The rest mass of the omega baryon is much larger than that of the proton. Discuss how energy and momentum are conserved in the collision.
questions.answer: The kinetic energy of the incoming K meson is converted into rest mass energy of the new particles, and total momentum is the same before and after the collision.
steps: Total energy is conserved: the K meson kinetic energy plus rest energies of the initial particles equals the total energy of the products.
Producing a heavier omega baryon needs more energy, which comes from the kinetic energy of the incoming K meson.
Momentum is conserved: the initial momentum of the K meson is shared among the products, which move off in directions that add to the original momentum.
Because the proton is at rest, the total initial momentum equals that of the incoming K meson.
The vectors of the product momenta must sum to this value, so the tracks must be arranged to balance momentum.
The energy needed exceeds the rest energies of the proton and K meson, so the K meson must be moving fast enough.

questions.question: Explain why GeV/c is a valid unit for momentum.
questions.answer: GeV is a unit of energy and c is a speed, and energy / speed has the base units kg m s^-1, which are the units of momentum (as in E = pc, so p = E / c).
steps: The electronvolt, and so the GeV, is a unit of energy: 1 GeV = 1.6 x 10^-10 J.
c is a speed, so GeV/c is a unit of energy divided by speed.
Base units: J / (m s^-1) = (kg m^2 s^-2) / (m s^-1) = kg m s^-1.
kg m s^-1 is the unit of momentum (p = m v), so GeV/c is a valid unit for momentum; this matches p = E / c for a relativistic particle.

questions.question: A storage ring has circumference 44.7 m and field 1.45 T. The website says it confines muons of momentum 3.10 GeV/c (= 1.65 x 10^-18 N s). Deduce whether the claim is correct, given muon charge -1.6 x 10^-19 C.
questions.answer: Correct: the radius from p = B q r is 7.1 m, which matches the circumference 44.7 m / (2 pi) = 7.1 m.
steps: Circumference 44.7 m gives radius r = 44.7 / (2 pi) = 7.11 m.
Required momentum: p = B |q| r = 1.45 x 1.6 x 10^-19 x 7.11 = 1.65 x 10^-18 N s.
This equals 3.10 GeV/c (3.10 x 10^9 x 1.6 x 10^-19 / 3.00 x 10^8 = 1.65 x 10^-18 N s), so the claim is correct.

questions.question: Stationary muons have a mean lifetime of a few microseconds, but muons in the ring have a much greater mean lifetime. Explain why.

questions.question: Deduce which collision is more likely to produce new particles with the largest mass: a high energy electron hitting a stationary atom, or head-on beams of electrons colliding.
questions.answer: Head-on colliding beams: their total momentum is zero, so all the energy is available to create mass, whereas a stationary target leaves kinetic energy in the products.
steps: In a collision with a stationary target, momentum must be conserved, so the products keep some kinetic energy.
This kinetic energy cannot be used to create mass.
In head-on collisions the total momentum is zero, so the products can be at rest in the centre-of-momentum frame.
All the collision energy is then available for rest mass, so head-on beams produce the largest new masses.

questions.question: The mass of the Z boson is 91 GeV/c^2. Show that it is nearly 100 times the mass of a proton.
questions.answer: Proton mass = 0.94 GeV/c^2, so 91 / 0.94 = 97, nearly 100 times.
steps: So the Z boson is nearly 100 times the mass of the proton.

questions.question: Explain why the protons and antiprotons needed high energies to produce the Z boson.
questions.answer: The collision energy must supply the rest energy of the Z boson (91 GeV), which requires high kinetic energy in the beams.
steps: A Z boson has rest energy 91 GeV, so the collision must supply at least this energy.
Mass is created from energy via E = m c^2, so the energy must come from the kinetic energy of the colliding particles.
High energy beams give the required total energy in the collision.

questions.question: Z bosons produced by high energy collisions have a range of lifetimes. Those with the longest lifetimes were moving very fast. Explain this observation.
questions.answer: Time dilation: a fast moving Z boson has a lifetime that is gamma times its rest lifetime in the laboratory frame.
steps: A Z boson moving at high speed has gamma > 1.
In the laboratory frame its lifetime is t = gamma tau, which is longer than its rest lifetime.
So the fastest moving Z bosons have the longest observed lifetimes.

questions.question: Which row in the table gives the charge and mass of an antiproton? (The table is not in the text.)
questions.answer: Pending: the table of options is missing. Physics: charge -e, mass equal to the proton.

questions.question: An alpha particle with kinetic energy 5.52 MeV approaches a gold nucleus head on and is brought to rest. Calculate the minimum distance between them.
questions.answer: Minimum distance = 4.1 x 10^-14 m
steps: At the closest point all kinetic energy is electric potential energy: E k = k (2e)(79e) / r.

questions.question: The minimum distance between an alpha particle and a gold nucleus is 5.68 x 10^-14 m. Calculate the maximum electrostatic force between them.
questions.answer: F = 11 N
steps: Maximum force occurs at the minimum distance: F = k Q q / r^2.

questions.question: Explain why the existence of a sixth quark was predicted, given that five quarks were known in 1977.
questions.answer: The standard model has leptons in pairs (three generations), so symmetry with quarks requires six quarks.
steps: Leptons are known to form pairs (electron/neutrino and muon/neutrino etc.), giving six leptons.
The quark-lepton model is symmetric, so quarks should also come in pairs and generations.
With five quarks known, a sixth quark (the top) was predicted to complete the symmetry.

questions.question: Name the two categories of hadron.
questions.answer: Baryons and mesons.
steps: Hadrons are composite particles made of quarks.
They are divided into baryons (three quarks) and mesons (quark and antiquark).

questions.question: Explain the advantage of colliding beams of particles travelling in opposite directions rather than directing a beam at a stationary target.
questions.answer: In head-on collisions the total momentum is zero, so all the energy can be used to create new particles; a stationary target wastes energy on the momentum of the products.
steps: With a stationary target, momentum conservation means the products must keep some kinetic energy.
With colliding beams of equal momentum, the total momentum is zero.
The products can then be at rest in the centre-of-momentum frame, so all the collision energy goes to rest mass.
Therefore more mass can be produced for the same beam energy.

questions.question: Protons and antiprotons each have total energy 900 GeV in a collider. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy, in joules, of a top quark produced (rest energy 173 GeV).
questions.answer: Maximum kinetic energy = 727 GeV = 1.2 x 10^-7 J
steps: Head-on equal energy beams: total momentum zero, so the top and anti-top each share total energy 900 GeV.
Maximum kinetic energy of a top quark: 900 - 173 = 727 GeV.

questions.question: Deduce whether a top quark with kinetic energy 1.2 x 10^-7 J is travelling at a relativistic speed (rest mass 173 GeV/c^2).
questions.answer: Yes: rest energy is 2.8 x 10^-8 J, so the kinetic energy is about 4.3 times the rest energy, gamma = 5.3 and v = 0.98c.
steps: This is a relativistic speed.

questions.question: Most quarks form hadrons in about 10^-23 s, but the top quark lifetime is 10^-25 s. Assess the student's suggestion that relativistic top quarks might form hadrons.
questions.answer: Unlikely at the speeds found: the dilation factor (gamma about 5) gives a lifetime of about 5 x 10^-25 s, far below 10^-23 s; a gamma near 100 would be needed.
steps: Relativistic time dilation increases the lifetime by gamma.
Required lifetime is about 10^-23 s, so gamma must be about 10^-23 / 10^-25 = 100.
The top quark in part (b)(iii) has gamma about 5, giving lifetime about 5 x 10^-25 s, still too short.
The suggestion is therefore not supported unless the top quarks move at speeds much closer to c.

questions.question: A particle with charge Q and momentum p follows a circular path of radius r at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density B. Derive the equation r = p / (Q B).
questions.answer: r = p / (Q B)
steps: Magnetic force provides centripetal force: Q v B = m v^2 / r.
Rearrange: r = m v / (Q B).
Momentum p = m v, so r = p / (Q B).

questions.question: An alpha particle of energy 5.4 MeV follows a circular path of radius 0.096 m. Calculate B (alpha mass 6.64 x 10^-27 kg).
steps: Charge Q = 2e = 3.2 x 10^-19 C.

questions.question: State one difference between a positron and an electron.
questions.answer: The positron has charge +e and the electron has charge -e.
steps: The positron is the antiparticle of the electron.
Its charge is +e, while the electron's charge is -e.

questions.question: Explain why electrons are deflected into a parabolic path when a potential difference is applied between plates A and B.
questions.answer: The electric field between the plates is uniform, giving a constant downward force, while the horizontal velocity is constant, so the path is a parabola like projectile motion.
steps: The electric field between the parallel plates is uniform and perpendicular to the beam.
The force F = e E on each electron is constant, so the vertical acceleration is constant.
The horizontal velocity stays constant because there is no horizontal force.
Constant horizontal velocity with constant vertical acceleration gives a parabolic path.

questions.question: Show that the maximum speed of electrons accelerated through 850 V from the cathode to the anode is about 1.7 x 10^7 m s^-1.
steps: Work done on each electron = eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 850 = 1.36 x 10^-16 J.
This becomes kinetic energy: 0.5 m v^2 = eV, so v = sqrt(2 e V / m).

questions.question: The electric field between the plates is 1.7 x 10^4 V m^-1 and each plate is 7.5 cm long. Electrons enter horizontally at the maximum speed (1.7 x 10^7 m s^-1). Calculate the vertical deflection of the beam, ignoring weight.
questions.answer: Vertical deflection = 2.8 x 10^-2 m (about 2.8 cm)
steps: Vertical acceleration: a = e E / m = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 1.7 x 10^4 / 9.11 x 10^-31 = 3.0 x 10^15 m s^-2.
Time between plates: t = L / v = 0.075 / 1.73 x 10^7 = 4.3 x 10^-9 s.

questions.question: The electric field is removed and a uniform magnetic field of 3.0 mT makes the beam follow a circle of radius 3.5 cm. Assess whether this gives a specific charge (e/m) in agreement with the standard value (1.76 x 10^11 C kg^-1).
questions.answer: e/m = 1.6 x 10^11 C kg^-1, about 7 percent below the standard 1.76 x 10^11 C kg^-1, so it is in reasonable agreement given the approximations.
steps: For circular motion: e v B = m v^2 / r, so e/m = v / (B r).
Standard value 1.76 x 10^11 C kg^-1 is used for comparison (not in the text).
The difference is about 6 to 7 percent, which is reasonable agreement given measurement uncertainties in r and B.

questions.question: Which of the following is a fundamental particle? A: neutrino; B: neutron; C: pion; D: proton.
questions.answer: A: neutrino
steps: The neutron, pion and proton are made of quarks, so they are not fundamental.
The neutrino is a lepton, which is fundamental.

questions.question: Give a possible quark structure of a pion.
questions.answer: pi^+ = u d-bar (up quark and anti-down quark)
steps: Pions are mesons made of one quark and one antiquark.
A pi^+ is an up quark and an anti-down quark: charge +2/3 + 1/3 = +1.

questions.question: A pion decays into a muon and an antineutrino. Energy and momentum are conserved. Explain two other conservation laws that apply to this decay.
questions.answer: Charge and lepton number are conserved (baryon number, 0 to 0, is also conserved).
steps: Charge: a pi^- (charge -1) decays to mu^- (-1) plus an antineutrino (0), so charge is conserved.
Lepton number: the muon (+1) and antineutrino (-1) give total 0, matching the pion's lepton number 0.
Baryon number is 0 on both sides, so it is conserved too.

questions.question: A muon has mass 106 MeV/c^2. Calculate its mass in kg.
A pion at rest has an average lifetime of 26 ns. High energy pions in the atmosphere have speeds up to 0.99c. Explain how their average lifetime compares with the rest lifetime.
questions.answer: Their average lifetime is longer, by a factor gamma of about 7 at 0.99c, because of time dilation.
steps: At 0.99c the Lorentz factor gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - 0.99^2) = 7.1.
Time dilation makes the observed lifetime gamma times the rest lifetime.
So the high energy pions last about 7 times longer than pions at rest.

q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C (positive particle).

questions.question: The positive particle is made of two up quarks and one strange quark. State what type of particle it is.
questions.answer: A baryon (it is a Sigma-plus baryon, uus).
steps: Three quarks make a baryon, and two up plus one strange gives uus.
So the particle is a baryon (a Sigma-plus hyperon).

questions.question: Amaterasu had energy 2.4 x 10^20 eV, said to equal a 2.8 kg brick dropped from waist height 1.1 m. Deduce whether the article is correct.
questions.answer: Approximately correct: 2.4 x 10^20 eV = 38 J, while the brick's energy mgh = 30 J, which agree within about 25 percent.
steps: Gravitational potential energy: E = m g h = 2.8 x 9.81 x 1.1 = 30 J.
38 J and 30 J are the same order of magnitude, so the article is approximately correct.

questions.question: Explain the quark structure of a K minus meson.
questions.answer: A K minus meson is a strange quark and an anti-up quark (s u-bar), with total charge -1.
steps: A K minus is a meson, so it is one quark and one antiquark.
Charge -1 = strange (-1/3) + anti-up (-2/3), so the structure is s u-bar.

questions.question: Explain how the cyclotron produces a beam of high energy particles, referring to the alternating p.d. and the magnetic field.
questions.answer: The magnetic field makes particles move in circles, and the alternating p.d. across the dee gap accelerates them once per half turn, so they spiral outwards to high energy.
steps: The magnetic field makes charged particles move in circles inside the dees.
The alternating p.d. across the gap accelerates the particles each time they cross it.
The p.d. frequency matches the cyclotron frequency, which is independent of speed.
Energy increases each crossing, so the radius grows and particles leave as a high energy beam.

questions.question: The high energy electrons in the LHeC have energy 60 GeV. Show that they are travelling at relativistic speeds.
questions.answer: gamma = 60 000 / 0.511 = 1.2 x 10^5, so the electrons travel at a speed indistinguishable from c.
steps: Electron rest energy: m c^2 = 0.511 MeV.
Since gamma is much greater than 1, the electrons are ultra-relativistic, with speed very close to c.

questions.question: Explain how a linac produces high energy electrons, referring to the a.c. supply and to the lengths of the drift tubes in the start and end sections.
questions.answer: The alternating p.d. accelerates electrons in each gap; drift tubes are short at the start where electrons are slow and long at the end where they are fast, keeping the timing in step with the constant frequency.
steps: The electrons are accelerated across each gap between drift tubes by the alternating p.d.
Inside the drift tubes the field is zero, so electrons move at constant speed.
At the start the electrons are slow, so the tubes are short to match half a period.
As electrons speed up, the tubes get longer, keeping the time in each tube equal to half the fixed a.c. period.
So the field reverses in step with the electrons at each gap, and the electrons gain energy at every gap.
Repeated acceleration gives very high energy electrons.

questions.question: Explain why high energies are required to investigate the structure of protons.
questions.answer: High energy gives a short de Broglie wavelength, so the probe can resolve detail as small as quarks inside protons, and provides energy to create new particles.
steps: The probe must have a wavelength smaller than the proton to resolve its structure.
The de Broglie wavelength lambda = h / p is short when the momentum is high.
High energy means high momentum and so a short wavelength.
The energy is also needed to overcome forces and create new particles.

questions.question: State the quark structure of baryons and of mesons.
questions.answer: Baryon: three quarks. Meson: one quark and one antiquark.
steps: Baryons are made of three quarks.
Mesons are made of a quark and an antiquark.

questions.question: In 1934 Chadwick fired alpha particles at beryllium atoms, producing carbon atoms and neutral particles. Complete the equation for this process.

Products: carbon 12/6 C plus neutron 1/0 n, which gives mass number 13 and proton number 6.

questions.question: Criticise the statement that Chadwick's experiment established the neutron as a new fundamental particle and not an electron and proton joined together.
questions.answer: The neutron is not fundamental: it is a composite baryon made of one up and two down quarks, so the experiment did not establish that it is fundamental.
steps: The neutron is a baryon made of three quarks (udd), so it is not a fundamental particle.
Chadwick's experiment showed that a neutral particle of about proton mass exists, but not that it is fundamental.
The statement is therefore incorrect as a conclusion about the structure of the neutron.

questions.question: Some muons are produced 15 000 m above the ground and travel vertically downwards. Explain why most reach the ground before decaying.
questions.answer: Time dilation: at speeds close to c the lifetime seen from the ground is gamma times longer, so the muons travel many kilometres before decaying.
steps: Without time dilation a muon at 0.98c would travel only about 650 m before decaying, which is far less than 15 000 m.
At speeds close to c, gamma is large, so the ground-frame lifetime is gamma x 2.2 x 10^-6 s.
For 15 000 m at 0.98c, gamma must be about 23 or more (speed about 0.999c), so the lifetime is long enough.
Hence most muons reach the ground before decaying.

questions.question: Which of the following is a meson? A: photon; B: pion; C: positron; D: proton.
questions.answer: B: pion
steps: A photon is a boson, a fundamental particle, not a meson.
A positron is a lepton and a proton is a baryon.
A pion is a meson, made of a quark and an antiquark.

questions.question: In pair production a photon creates an electron and a positron. Which gives the photon energy in joules? A: 9.11e-31 x (3e8)^2; B: 1.67e-27 x (3e8)^2; C: 2 x 1.67e-27 x (3e8)^2; D: 2 x 9.11e-31 x (3e8)^2.
steps: Pair production needs the photon to supply the rest energy of both the electron and positron: E = 2 m_e c^2.
Option D uses the electron mass (9.11 x 10^-31 kg) twice, giving the correct energy.
Options A and B use only one electron or a proton mass, and C uses the proton mass.

questions.question: Two protons react to form a proton, a neutron, a positron and an electron neutrino. Explain how three conservation laws apply to this reaction, other than energy and momentum.
questions.answer: Charge (2 = 2), baryon number (2 = 2), and lepton number (0 = -1 + 1 = 0) are all conserved.
steps: Charge: left = +1 + 1 = +2; right = +1 (proton) + 0 (neutron) + 1 (positron) + 0 (neutrino) = +2, conserved.
Baryon number: left = 1 + 1 = 2; right = 1 (proton) + 1 (neutron) = 2, conserved.
Lepton number: left = 0; right = -1 (positron) + 1 (electron neutrino) = 0, conserved.

questions.question: An electron and a positron annihilate, producing two photons. Which gives the energy of one photon? A: 9.11e-31 x (3e8)^2; B: 9.11e-31 x 3e8; C: 2 x 9.11e-31 x (3e8)^2; D: 2 x 9.11e-31 x 3e8.
steps: Total energy from annihilation = 2 m_e c^2, shared equally between the two photons.
Each photon has energy m_e c^2 = 9.11 x 10^-31 x (3 x 10^8)^2, which is option A.
Option C gives the total energy, not one photon.

questions.question: Explain how conservation of baryon number and conservation of charge are obeyed in the reaction K^- + p -> Omega^- + K^+ + K^0.
questions.answer: Baryon number: 1 (proton) = 1 (Omega minus); charge: -1 + 1 = 0 = -1 + 1 + 0.
steps: Baryon number: the proton has baryon number +1; the Omega minus has +1; the kaons have 0. So 1 = 1.
Both conservation laws are obeyed.

questions.question: The predicted mass of the Omega minus was 2.9714 x 10^-27 kg, and the accepted value is 1672 MeV/c^2. Calculate the percentage difference between these masses.
